stimulus.text:
“The first question that presents itself on the subject is, whether a confederated government be the best for the United States or not? Or in other words, whether the thirteen United States should be reduced to one great republic, governed by one legislature, and under the direction of one executive and judicial; or whether they should continue thirteen confederated republics, under the direction and controul of a supreme federal head for certain defined national purposes only? . . . This government is to possess absolute and uncontroulable power, legislative, executive and judicial, with respect to every object to which it extends, for by the last clause of section 8th, article 1st, it is declared ‘that the Congress shall have power to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers.’”

—Brutus, No. 1, New-York Journal, October 18, 1787

books.section: Topic 3.8 The Constitutional Convention and Debates over Ratification, C. Federalists, Anti-Federalists, and the Adoption of the Bill of Rights

stem: Brutus, the author of this essay, is best described as

options.misconception: Brutus attacks the Constitution; the Federalists defended it.

options.text: A British official reporting on the Convention
options.misconception: Brutus wrote for New York readers about ratification, not as a British official.

options.text: A delegate who signed the Constitution at Philadelphia
options.misconception: Brutus opposed the finished Constitution; the signers supported it.

options.text: An Anti-Federalist writing against ratification of the Constitution

rationales.D: Brutus wrote against the proposed Constitution in the New York press during the ratification debate, which is the Anti-Federalist position.
rationales.A: Background: the Federalists defended the Constitution; Brutus attacks it.
rationales.B: Brutus was an American writing for New York readers, not a British official.
rationales.C: Brutus opposed the finished document. Background: its signers had supported it.
rationales.general:
1. The essay appeared in a New York newspaper while the state debated ratification.
2. Its argument is against the Constitution as a consolidated government.
3. Background: opponents of ratification were called Anti-Federalists, and Brutus was one of their sharpest voices.
4. The Federalists defended the Constitution, so Brutus cannot be one of them.
Remember: the side a writer argues for names the writer's camp.
